results.q: What happens when a message is posted to a queue that is already full?
answer: This is handled in OSQPost() (Source/os_q.c:672): it checks `pq->OSQEntries >= pq->OSQSize`, and when that is true it calls CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and calls CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and returns `(OS_ERR_Q_FULL)`, so the rest of OSQPost() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT — the previous values stay in place.

results.q: What happens when a task asks for a memory block and the partition has none left?
answer: This is handled in OSTCBInitHook() (Ports/Win32/Visual Studio/os_cpu_c.c:594): it checks `p_stk->ThreadHandle == NULL`, and when that is true it calls CloseHandle() and calls CloseHandle() and records it (`p_stk->SignalPtr = NULL`, `p_stk->InitSignalPtr = NULL`) and returns immediately, so the rest of OSTCBInitHook() is skipped.

results.q: What happens when a task waiting on a semaphore times out?
answer: I could not find any code that detects the data stopping (no timeout or last-update check). If the data stops, the last received values would simply stay in place.

OSSemPend() would simply stop being called. It is called by OSTmr_Task() at Source/os_tmr.c:1112 with (`OSTmrSemSignal`, `0u`, `&err`), repeatedly inside `for (;;)`; OSTmr_Task() at Source/os_tmr.c:1112 with (`OSTmrSemSignal`, `0u`, `&err`), repeatedly inside `for (;;)`. The full chain from the program's start is: OSTaskW32() → OSTmr_Task() → OSSemPend().

results.q: What happens when OSSemPend is called from an ISR?
answer: This is handled in OSSemPend() (Source/os_sem.c:351): it checks `OSIntNesting > 0u`, and when that is true it returns immediately, so the rest of OSSemPend() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: CPU_CRITICAL_ENTER, CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT — the previous values stay in place.

results.q: What happens when a task waits for a mutex that a lower-priority task owns?
answer: This is handled in OSMutexPend() (Source/os_mutex.c:517): it checks `(INT8U)(pevent->OSEventCnt & OS_MUTEX_KEEP_LOWER_8) == OS_MUTEX_AVAILABLE`, and when that is true it sets `pevent->OSEventCnt &= OS_MUTEX_KEEP_UPPER_8` (line 518); then it sets `pevent->OSEventCnt |= (INT16U)OSTCBCur->OSTCBPrio` (line 519); then it sets `pevent->OSEventPtr = (void *)OSTCBCur` (line 520); then it checks `(pcp != OS_PRIO_MUTEX_CEIL_DIS) && (OSTCBCur->OSTCBPrio <= pcp)` (line 521); if true it calls CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and sets `*perr = OS_ERR_PCP_LOWER`; then it calls CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT (line 526); then it sets `*perr = OS_ERR_NONE` (line 527); then it returns immediately, so the rest of OSMutexPend() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: OS_EventTaskWait(), CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT, OSRdyGrp, OSRdyTbl, OSTCBPrioTbl — the previous values stay in place.

Consequence: OSMboxPost() checks `pevent->OSEventPtr != (void *)0` (Source/os_mbox.c:553); `pevent->OSEventPtr != (void *)0` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and may call CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and may call CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT.

Consequence: OSMboxPostOpt() checks `pevent->OSEventPtr != (void *)0` (Source/os_mbox.c:640); `pevent->OSEventPtr != (void *)0` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and may call CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT and may call CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT.
Consequence: OSEventPendMulti() checks `pevent->OSEventCnt > 0u` (Source/os_core.c:414); `pevent->OSEventCnt > 0u` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping CPU_CRITICAL_EXIT.

results.q: Where is the system time OSTime incremented?
answer: OSTime is a global variable of type `volatile INT32U`, defined in Source/ucos_ii.h:760 — the code describes it as: "Current value of system time (in ticks)".
It is set by OSTimeTick() (`OSTime++`, line 954); OS_InitMisc() (`OSTime = 0uL`, line 1392); OSTimeSet() (`OSTime = ticks`, line 276).
It is read by OSTimeTick() (line 954), OSTimeGet() (line 247).

In short: OSTime carries a value produced by OSTimeSet(), OSTimeTick(), OS_InitMisc() and consumed by OSTimeGet(), OSTimeTick(). OSTimeTick() both reads and updates it, so it also keeps state between calls.
